growth_story.headline: Somalia's income per person rose fast from 2010 to 2017, then slipped and has stayed broadly flat as drought and swings in foreign aid weigh on the economy.
growth_story.arc: From 1990 to 1997 income per person fell 1.6 percent a year, as the government was toppled in 1991 and the country slid into a long civil war; the worst single year was 1994, at -21.9 percent. Growth turned positive from 1998 to 2009, at 3.3 percent a year, though the sources say little about this period and official GDP figures have only been compiled since 2012, on broad assumptions. From 2010 to 2017 growth rose to 6.1 percent a year, an era that includes the formation of a federal government in 2012 and the start of rebuilding state institutions, and income per person peaked in 2017. Since 2018 growth has averaged -1.0 percent a year, with a fall of 6.4 percent in 2020, and income per person is now 8.1 percent below its 2017 peak, about where it first was in 2016. World Bank and IMF reports point to repeated droughts, heavy reliance on aid and imports, and sharp aid cuts in 2025: the economy has kept growing, but income per person has stayed broadly flat.

threads.title: State collapse and civil war
threads.text: In 1991 armed groups toppled the government and the central state fell apart. Years of conflict followed, and the World Bank describes how recurring cycles of conflict and instability undid earlier gains. This is the backdrop to the falls of the early 1990s.

citations.title: Federal Republic of Somalia: Systematic Country Diagnostic
citations.quote: since the collapse of the Somali state in 1991, recurrent cycles of conflict and instability have often undone any progress achieved.

threads.title: Rebuilding the state after 2012
threads.text: A provisional constitution was adopted in 2012 and a new federal government formed, which began rebuilding state institutions and infrastructure. This rebuilding falls within the fastest era in the data, 2010 to 2017.

citations.title: Somalia: Staff-Monitored Program—Press Release; and Staff Report (IMF Country Report No. 16/136)
citations.quote: Since 2012, the federal government has embarked on a process of rebuilding state institutions and rehabilitating the economic and social infrastructure.

citations.title: Somalia: Staff-Monitored Program—Press Release; and Staff Report (IMF Country Report No. 16/136)
citations.quote: A provisional constitution was adopted in August 2012 and traditional elders across the country elected a 275-member Federal Parliament.

threads.title: Droughts that strike every few years
threads.text: Severe droughts hit Somalia every few years, including the 2011/12 famine and the 2016/17 drought. Failed rains in 2025 again cut crops and livestock and helped slow the economy.

citations.title: Federal Republic of Somalia: Systematic Country Diagnostic
citations.quote: strikes every few years with particularly severe consequences, as seen in the 2011/2 famine and 2016/7 drought.

citations.title: Somalia Economic Update, May 2026: Navigating Shocks, Powering Growth (Edition 11)
citations.quote: Somalia’s economic growth moderated in 2025 on the back of a sharp decline in foreign aid and drought conditions.

threads.title: Dependence on aid and imports
threads.text: Somalia has relied on foreign aid for security and humanitarian support, so swings in aid move household spending and demand. Aid was cut sharply in 2025, and the IMF lists further aid cuts among the high risks ahead.

citations.title: Macro Poverty Outlook: Somalia
citations.quote: Declining and volatile foreign aid translates into unpredictable humanitarian assistance and volatile aggregate demand, and threatens to reverse gains in poverty reduction.

citations.title: Somalia Economic Update, May 2026: Navigating Shocks, Powering Growth (Edition 11)
citations.quote: The withdrawal of humanitarian and security-related assistance reduced aggregate demand, while adverse weather conditions disrupted agricultural and livestock production.

citations.title: IMF Staff Concludes 2026 Article IV Consultation Mission to Somalia
citations.quote: Near-term risks identified as high include more severe climate shocks, renewed regional conflict, further aid retrenchment

threads.title: Debt relief and reform
threads.text: Somalia reached the end point of the debt relief process for heavily indebted poor countries in December 2023, and nearly all of its old foreign debt was wiped out. The World Bank calls this a turning point for the public finances; income per person has stayed broadly flat since.

citations.title: Somalia Economic Update, May 2026: Navigating Shocks, Powering Growth (Edition 11)
citations.quote: Somalia’s attainment of the HIPC Completion Point in December 2023 has marked a turning point, restoring fiscal space, improving debt sustainability, and strengthening macroeconomic credibility.

citations.title: Somalia Economic Update, May 2026: Navigating Shocks, Powering Growth (Edition 11)
citations.quote: Nearly all legacy external debt was eliminated, the largest of which was debt to Paris Club countries

since_last_year.text: Over the past year the economy slowed. Aid cuts in 2025 and a largely failed late-2025 rainy season hit spending, crops and livestock. In 2026 the conflict in the Middle East pushed up food, fuel and transport costs, and the World Bank (October 2026) expects growth to slow again in 2026.

citations.quote: below-average Gu rains and a largely failed Deyr season led to severe pasture and water shortages

citations.title: Macro Poverty Outlook: Somalia
citations.quote: The prolonged Middle East conflict has contributed to higher food, fuel, and transport costs, while drought conditions constrain agricultural output.

citations.title: Macro Poverty Outlook: Somalia
citations.quote: Real GDP growth is expected to slow from 3.1 percent in 2025 to 2.5 percent in 2026

growth_story.tension: The sources report steady GDP growth from 2023 to 2025, but the data show income per person barely moving (1.0, 0.5 and -0.4 percent), because the population is growing almost as fast as the economy. The World Bank itself calls real GDP per capita "broadly stagnant". The older figures are also fragile. The IMF noted in 2016 that Somalia's GDP figures had been compiled since 2012 on broad assumptions, and the data show income per person jumping 10.4 percent in 2017, a year the World Bank describes as one of severe drought.
